name: British Virgin Islands
summary_text: Same-sex intimacy has not been a criminal offence in the British Virgin Islands since January 2001, when the United Kingdom's Privy Council ordered the repeal of the sodomy laws in the territory and four other remaining British Caribbean territories after the local legislatures declined to act. Local legislator Orlando Smith conceded the position publicly, stating that "there is nothing we can do." The decriminalisation arrived by order of the United Kingdom's highest court of appeal rather than by enactment of the local House of Assembly.  The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010, including its 2025 single-sex-services code, does not automatically apply in the British Virgin Islands. The territory stands under the United Kingdom's constitutional framework, and measures of the United Kingdom's Parliament extend to it only when brought into force by Order in Council. A trans visitor should not assume the Equality Act's discrimination and service-access protections are available there by default; any such protection must be traced to British Virgin Islands legislation or to a specific extension order.  Family status remains contested rather than settled. The case testing whether the United Kingdom same-sex marriage of Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome is valid under British Virgin Islands law was still running when, on 29 July 2022, the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal the case-management orders of Justice Adrian Jack, as reported by BVI News. That refusal cleared a procedural obstacle and left the proceedings in place; it is not itself a ruling on whether such a marriage is recognised in the territory.

name: Wallis and Futuna
summary_text: Wallis and Futuna is a territorial collectivity of the French Republic and stands under the French national framework: the civil and criminal codes of France apply locally unless a local measure overrides them. No law in force criminalises trans people or same-sex relations, and discrimination on grounds of gender identity has been prohibited since the 2012 statutory extension covering employment, housing and access to services.  Legal gender-marker change is available on the basis of the 2016-17 French reforms, which removed the requirement for surgery or a psychiatric diagnosis. A trans visitor whose documents already reflect their lived gender can present them without entering a separate local procedure. French law recognises no non-binary status, so a third-gender or X marker cannot be obtained.  Nothing in the sources indicates trans-specific screening at entry or in local administrative processing. Practical exposure to harm is concentrated in two areas: detention and everyday social conditions. Under the French prison framework that applies here, trans women whose legal gender is marked male, largely those without reassignment surgery, are held in all-male establishments, a situation described in reporting as a documented legal grey area; one such transfer to a men's facility in Lille took place in 2014.

sources.documents: Decriminalisation of same-sex sexual activity in private in France, retained in 1810 Code and followed in French colonies; foundational legal status applicable to Wallis and Futuna as French territory.

sources.documents: Allows transgender people to legally change gender without surgery or sterilisation, via court order from 1 January 2017; no psychiatrist certificates or proof of surgery required, first-name change via registry office.
